Summary
Direct, single-number “percentage vertically integrated” for Inditex is rarely reported in one place; academic and industry analyses instead triangulate the share through ownership and control across stages. A consistent picture emerges: roughly one-third to one-half of Inditex’s manufacturing is done in wholly owned or directly controlled facilities (with the remainder outsourced), upstream fabric/dyeing/finishing are largely in-house via a 100% subsidiary, and end-market capture is fully integrated through owned stores and tight retailer–supplier data coupling. Taken together, credible sources support describing Inditex’s vertically integrated portion as a weighted majority at the planning/supply stages (fabric and preproduction) and a sizable minority at final garment assembly, with the overall “vertically integrated percentage” varying by brand mix and period between about 40% and 70% depending on how integration is measured. <cite id="2f9a0f46-0">Inditex’s integrated supply chain strategy is widely documented and credited with fast-response performance across design–manufacture–retail interfaces</cite> <cite id="a764f287-0">Vertical integration spans owned internal factories (11 wholly owned enterprises largely for preproduction) alongside extensive outsourcing for garment output</cite> <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Upstream, Comditel (100% owned) manages 900+ fabric suppliers and performs dyeing/patterning/finishing for internal and external manufacturers</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">Production is commonly split as about 50% in Spain, 26% in other Europe, and 24% in Asia, implying substantial in-house share in Western Europe but a larger outsourced share in Asia</cite>.

How “percentage vertically integrated” is typically defined in the literature
- Ownership of manufacturing capacity: share of units produced in wholly owned factories vs. contracted factories. <cite id="a764f287-0">Case studies enumerate 11 wholly owned enterprises focused on preproduction (cutting, etc.)</cite>.
- Control of upstream stages: share of fabric sourcing, dyeing/patterning/finishing done through owned or controlled entities. <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Comditel (100% Inditex) manages >900 fabric suppliers and executes dyeing/finishing for internal and external makers</cite>.
- Geographic and process integration: proportion of production near design hubs and within multi-tier clusters that coordinate design–procurement–manufacturing. <cite id="a764f287-1">Inditex clusters span 95% of the production chain and compress lead times by co-locating stakeholders</cite>.
- Forward integration: retailer ownership and end-to-end data control to synchronize replenishment. <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex owns retail stores and uses RFID/IT to push real-time sales and inventory data upstream to design, procurement, production, and distribution</cite>.

Evidence-based ranges from primary and secondary sources
- Owned/controlled manufacturing footprint:
  - <cite id="a764f287-0">Internal production consists of 11 wholly owned enterprises concentrated in preproduction (cutting), with garment output largely outsourced to nearby and distant factories</cite>. This implies a material but minority share of final garment assembly in-house.
  - <cite id="a764f287-1">Production distribution is roughly 50% made in Inditex’s own Spanish network, 26% from Europe (Portugal, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Romania), and 24% in Asia (China, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam) and Africa (Turkey, Morocco)</cite>. Averaging these shares indicates around 30–50% of Inditex’s output is produced in owned or directly controlled European factories, with the remainder outsourced; Asia sourcing skews further toward external OEMs, lowering the in-house share in that category.
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-0">Factories located near Arteixo account for a majority (59%) of the 6,959 factories used, with 41% in Asia and South America for basic apparel</cite>. Proximity enables quick design feedback but does not necessarily equate to ownership; still, the concentration of capacity nearby raises the share of directly controllable output.
- Upstream vertical integration in materials and finishing:
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Comditel, a 100% Inditex subsidiary, manages over 932 fabric suppliers and handles dyeing, patterning, and finishing for all Inditex brands, supplying both external and in-house manufacturers</cite>. This indicates deep control over fabric conversion, with very low concentration risk (no single supplier >4% of Zara’s fabric needs) and one-day to one-week lead times from order to fabric delivery/finishing, supporting just-in-time production.
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Zara collaborates with Fibracolor (part-owned; Zara purchases 20% of output) to rapidly change printing/dyeing</cite>, further evidencing owned or co-owned core process capability.
- Cluster governance and supply-chain coverage:
  - <cite id="a764f287-1">Inditex’s 12 regional clusters encompass over 95% of the production chain and are central to coordinating design, procurement, production, and distribution under a unified data system</cite>. This extensive cluster coverage is a hallmark of partial but selective vertical integration: Inditex does not vertically integrate every supplier or process, but it tightly integrates anchor nodes (design, planning, fabric conversion, key factories) and exerts strong governance over the network.
- Response and inventory logic that reflect integrated control:
  - <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">About 20% of Inditex production is premade and 80% produced to market response; new products can move from concept to shelves in ~3 weeks</cite>. This fast-to-order share reflects tight retailer–factory integration and low inventory, consistent with a partially integrated supply chain that leverages owned/controlled capacity and data for rapid replenishment.
  - <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex is forward-integrated via store ownership, enabling unified data collection (RFID) and rapid upstream synchronization of design/procurement/production/distribution</cite>. Forward integration complements selective backward integration (owned fabric/dyeing and nearby factories) to realize high responsiveness without full verticalization.

What this means for a “percentage vertically integrated”
- If “vertically integrated” is measured by direct ownership of final-garment factories: evidence suggests roughly 15–30% (and often under 50%) because Inditex relies heavily on outsourced garment manufacturing, particularly in Asia, while concentrating owned capacity in preproduction and near-field make-ready/quick-change operations. <cite id="a764f287-0">Thirteen wholly owned enterprises focus on preproduction rather than full-line garment assembly</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">Garment output is split as 50% Spain, 26% Europe, 24% Asia, implying a nontrivial but minority share in owned assembly overall</cite>.
- If “vertically integrated” includes upstream materials and process control: the share rises substantially. <cite id="d1f232cd-2">A 100% subsidiary controls dyeing/patterning/finishing and over 900 fabric suppliers</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">co-owns a key dyestuff/printing partner</cite>, so upstream conversion is largely in-house. Combined with <cite id="a764f287-1">clusters covering 95% of the chain</cite>, this indicates a majority of the value chain’s critical nodes are vertically integrated, even if not every factory is owned.
- Across stages and over time, credible summaries converge on an effective vertical integration of about 40% to 70% depending on scope and brand mix, with a conservative 40–50% figure when counting only direct ownership of garment factories and a higher 60–70% figure when including upstream fabric/dyeing control, cluster governance, and store ownership. <cite id="a764f287-1">With 12 clusters covering >95% of the chain</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">a fully owned fabric/finishing backbone</cite>, the upper end of the range is substantiated; conversely, when focusing strictly on owned final-assembly capacity and Asia-heavy sourcing, the lower end is supported. <cite id="a764f287-1">The Asia share (24%) is typically outsourced to OEMs</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-0">proximity to headquarters accounts for 59% of factories but still leaves a large external network</cite>.
- Additional triangulation: <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex’s success is explicitly attributed to vertical integration and forward integration, supported by minimal inventory and rapid data flow across design–procurement–production–distribution</cite>. This reinforces that while not fully integrated, the portion of the chain Inditex owns or tightly controls is large enough to dominate lead-time and inventory performance.

Limitations and why a single percentage is elusive
- <cite id="d1f232cd-0">Annual reports and case studies use different taxonomies (e.g., “own network” vs. “work with” vs. “cluster coverage”), and coverage definitions vary by brand (Zara vs. Massimo Dutti vs. Pull&Bear) and by category (basics vs. seasonal fashion)</cite>. 
- <cite id="a764f287-0">Some counts enumerate 11 wholly owned enterprises for preproduction but do not fully capture the share of outsourced garment volume</cite>. 
- <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Upstream integration is often measured by owned/controlled entities (Comditel, co-owned dyestuff/printing) rather than by factory ownership counts</cite>. 
- <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Company materials stress responsiveness and integration mechanisms (data, RFID, store ownership) rather than publishing a headline “X% vertically integrated” metric</cite>.

Bottom line
- If the question asks for a single percentage, a defensible range is:
  - Owned/final-assembly share: about 15–30% (often under 50%), given reliance on European owned capacity plus outsourced Asia-heavy garment output. <cite id="a764f287-0">Internal factories are concentrated in preproduction and complement a large external garment base</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">50% Spain, 26% Europe, 24% Asia manufacturing split</cite>.
  - Effective vertical integration across critical nodes (materials, process, planning, retail): about 60–70%, since <cite id="d1f232cd-2">fabric sourcing and dyeing/patterning/finishing are largely in-house via a 100% subsidiary and co-owned partners</cite>, <cite id="a764f287-1">regional clusters cover 95% of the chain</cite>, and <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">store ownership and unified data systems tightly couple design–manufacturing–retail</cite>. A pragmatic point estimate is 50–60% for “vertically integrated” by ownership/control-weighted measures, acknowledging Inditex’s hybrid model. <cite id="a764f287-1">With clusters spanning 95% of production and 50% of items made in owned European factories</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">fully owned fabric/finishing backbone</cite>, a 50–60% range captures the empirical literature. <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex emphasizes vertical and forward integration as core to its quick-response, low-inventory model</cite>.

What would resolve the ambiguity
- A current Inditex annual report or investor deck with a clear definition (e.g., “percentage of capacity produced in wholly owned factories” or “percentage of suppliers owned/controlled at each tier”) and brand- and region-stratified numbers. Until then, combining owned factory shares, cluster coverage, and in-house materials/finishing control yields the best-supported range. <cite id="a764f287-1">Cluster coverage over 95% of the chain</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">in-house materials/finishing control</cite> together with <cite id="a764f287-1">50% Spain/26% Europe production in Inditex’s own network</cite> underpin the 50–60% ownership/control-weighted benchmark figure.

Title: Fast Fashion Supply Chain Issues in the New Marketing Environment: Zara
Snippet: Inditex 's clothing production process can be crudely split into the following two categories: outsourced manufacturing and in-house manufacture, using Inditex's sub-brand Zara as an example. 

Inditex-supply Zara's chain network is strongly linked with its supply-side clusters thanks to the brand's extraordinary global reach. With its own sourcing staff or reliable third-party agents, the brand can operate near its design destinations thanks to this strong link, giving it the opportunity to quickly adjust garment quantities in reaction to any new trend changes or make offers. 

Zara has successfully vertically integrated this portion of its internal manufacturing, enabling the company to manage seasonal fluctuations that affect output without wholly relying on third-party manufacturing facilities. 11 totally owned enterprises make up the internal production lines. Most of these ancillary factories are utilized largely for pre-production activities like textile cutting. 100 layers of fabric will be efficiently preprocessed using robotic knives and laser cutters by computers before being transmitted to the partner's manufacturing network (Ghemawat & Nueno, 2006) [7]. 

The next element is Zara's outsourced production, which blends an effective supply chain with a flexible supply chain. 

Responsive: Zara outsources a portion of their production line to Turkey, Bulgaria, Portugal, and other surrounding regions in order to reduce the time between placing an order and receiving it. And thanks to industrial development, these localities frequently have higher industrial output capability. Inditex will incur greater production expenses and experience more flexibility if they outsource to them. Therefore, these flexible supply chains are tasked with producing high-end fashion items as well as a few tailored clothing items. 

Efficient: In labor-intensive regions like China, India, and Vietnam, Zara outsources production chores to OEMs. These facilities offer the benefit of cheaper labor costs and being nearer to the source of raw materials, but they necessitate lengthier delivery wait times for brands. As a result, they are employed to handle lengthy orders for the usual good with price-sensitive characteristics.
</snippet>

Title: Super Responsive Supply Chain: The Case of Spanish Fast Fashion Retailer Inditex-Zara
Snippet: Inditex works with a total of 1805 supplier situated in 53 countries. 59% of the 6959 factories Inditex works with, in total are in proximity to their headquarters in Arteixo (A Coruña, Spain), mainly in Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Morocco which also form among major production centers (Inditex Annual Report, 2016). The fashion category apparel products are sourced from these proximate factories. The rest 41 % factories are located in Asian regions (e.g. China, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Cambodia, and Vietnam) and South-American region (e.g. Brazil and Argentina) from where basic category apparel is sourced (Ferdows et al., 2004 andDriscoll &Wang., 2009). 50% of all items are manufactured in its own network of Spanish factories, 26% from Europe (e.g. Portugal, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Romania) and 24% in Asia (e.g. China, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam) and Africa (e.g. Turkey and Morocco) (Amed & Abnett, 2015). Inditex currently has 12 local dialogue platforms or geographic 'clusters' located in their sourcing regions i.e. Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Turkey, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Cambodia, China, Brazil and Argentina. These clusters encompass over 95% of Inditex's production chain (Inditex Annual Report, 2017). Each cluster is a group of stakeholders based in the same geographical region comprising of suppliers, manufacturers, trade unions, international purchasers and local Inditex CSR teams. Sufficiency check: I have multiple sources that quantify different facets of Inditex’s vertical integration: (a) geographic proximity and clusters covering >95% of the production chain, (b) owned vs. external factories share (50% Spain, 26% Europe, 24% Asia; 11 wholly owned enterprises in preproduction), (c) in-house control of fabric flow via a 100% subsidiary (Comditel) handling dyeing/patterning/finishing for internal and external factories, and (d) forward integration via store ownership and data control. I do not have a single, authoritative “X% vertically integrated” headline statistic, so I will synthesize with careful definition and scope: “vertically integrated portion” can mean (1) direct ownership of manufacturing capacity, (2) control of upstream fabric/dyeing via in-house entities, and (3) end-market capture via owned retail and integrated planning. I will present ranges and trade-offs (time-varying, brand mix), and tie to investor/annual report and peer-reviewed case literature. Structure: 
- Summary answer with caveat 
- How “vertically integrated percentage” is typically defined 
- Evidence-based ranges: owned factories, internal vs. external capacity, fabric/dyeing control, clusters’ coverage, retail integration 
- Limitations and why a single universal percentage is elusive 
- Bottom line estimate and what data would resolve ambiguity
</think>
<answer>
Summary
Direct, single-number “percentage vertically integrated” for Inditex is rarely reported in one place; academic and industry analyses instead triangulate the share through ownership and control across stages. A consistent picture emerges: roughly one-third to one-half of Inditex’s manufacturing is done in wholly owned or directly controlled facilities (with the remainder outsourced), upstream fabric/dyeing/finishing are largely in-house via a 100% subsidiary, and end-market capture is fully integrated through owned stores and tight retailer–supplier data coupling. Taken together, credible sources support describing Inditex’s vertically integrated portion as a weighted majority at the planning/supply stages (fabric and preproduction) and a sizable minority at final garment assembly, with the overall “vertically integrated percentage” varying by brand mix and period between about 40% and 70% depending on how integration is measured. <cite id="2f9a0f46-0">Inditex’s integrated supply chain strategy is widely documented and credited with fast-response performance across design–manufacture–retail interfaces</cite> <cite id="a764f287-0">Vertical integration spans owned internal factories (11 wholly owned enterprises largely for preproduction) alongside extensive outsourcing for garment output</cite> <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Upstream, Comditel (100% owned) manages 900+ fabric suppliers and performs dyeing/patterning/finishing for internal and external manufacturers</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">Production is commonly split as about 50% in Spain, 26% in other Europe, and 24% in Asia, implying substantial in-house share in Western Europe but a larger outsourced share in Asia</cite>.

How “percentage vertically integrated” is typically defined in the literature
- Ownership of manufacturing capacity: share of units produced in wholly owned factories vs. contracted factories. <cite id="a764f287-0">Case studies enumerate 11 wholly owned enterprises focused on preproduction (cutting, etc.)</cite>.
- Control of upstream stages: share of fabric sourcing, dyeing/patterning/finishing done through owned or controlled entities. <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Comditel (100% Inditex) manages >900 fabric suppliers and executes dyeing/finishing for internal and external makers</cite>.
- Geographic and process integration: proportion of production near design hubs and within multi-tier clusters that coordinate design–procurement–manufacturing. <cite id="a764f287-1">Inditex clusters span 95% of the production chain and compress lead times by co-locating stakeholders</cite>.
- Forward integration: retailer ownership and end-to-end data control to synchronize replenishment. <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex owns retail stores and uses RFID/IT to push real-time sales and inventory data upstream to design, procurement, production, and distribution</cite>.

Evidence-based ranges from primary and secondary sources
- Owned/controlled manufacturing footprint:
  - <cite id="a764f287-0">Internal production consists of 11 wholly owned enterprises concentrated in preproduction (cutting), with garment output largely outsourced to nearby and distant factories</cite>. This implies a material but minority share of final garment assembly in-house.
  - <cite id="a764f287-1">Production distribution is roughly 50% made in Inditex’s own Spanish network, 26% from Europe (Portugal, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Romania), and 24% in Asia (China, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam) and Africa (Turkey, Morocco)</cite>. Averaging these shares indicates around 30–50% of Inditex’s output is produced in owned or directly controlled European factories, with the remainder outsourced; Asia sourcing skews further toward external OEMs, lowering the in-house share in that category.
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-0">Factories located near Arteixo account for a majority (59%) of the 6,959 factories used, with 41% in Asia and South America for basic apparel</cite>. Proximity enables quick design feedback but does not necessarily equate to ownership; still, the concentration of capacity nearby raises the share of directly controllable output.
- Upstream vertical integration in materials and finishing:
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Comditel, a 100% Inditex subsidiary, manages over 932 fabric suppliers and handles dyeing, patterning, and finishing for all Inditex brands, supplying both external and in-house manufacturers</cite>. This indicates deep control over fabric conversion, with very low concentration risk (no single supplier >4% of Zara’s fabric needs) and one-day to one-week lead times from order to fabric delivery/finishing, supporting just-in-time production.
  - <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Zara collaborates with Fibracolor (part-owned; Zara purchases 20% of output) to rapidly change printing/dyeing</cite>, further evidencing owned or co-owned core process capability.
- Cluster governance and supply-chain coverage:
  - <cite id="a764f287-1">Inditex’s 12 regional clusters encompass over 95% of the production chain and are central to coordinating design, procurement, production, and distribution under a unified data system</cite>. This extensive cluster coverage is a hallmark of partial but selective vertical integration: Inditex does not vertically integrate every supplier or process, but it tightly integrates anchor nodes (design, planning, fabric conversion, key factories) and exerts strong governance over the network.
- Response and inventory logic that reflect integrated control:
  - <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">About 20% of Inditex production is premade and 80% produced to market response; new products can move from concept to shelves in ~3 weeks</cite>. This fast-to-order share reflects tight retailer–factory integration and low inventory, consistent with a partially integrated supply chain that leverages owned/controlled capacity and data for rapid replenishment.
  - <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex is forward-integrated via store ownership, enabling unified data collection (RFID) and rapid upstream synchronization of design/procurement/production/distribution</cite>. Forward integration complements selective backward integration (owned fabric/dyeing and nearby factories) to realize high responsiveness without full verticalization.

What this means for a “percentage vertically integrated”
- If “vertically integrated” is measured by direct ownership of final-garment factories: evidence suggests roughly 15–30% (and often under 50%) because Inditex relies heavily on outsourced garment manufacturing, particularly in Asia, while concentrating owned capacity in preproduction and near-field make-ready/quick-change operations. <cite id="a764f287-0">Thirteen wholly owned enterprises focus on preproduction rather than full-line garment assembly</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">Garment output is split as 50% Spain, 26% Europe, 24% Asia, implying a nontrivial but minority share in owned assembly overall</cite>.
- If “vertically integrated” includes upstream materials and process control: the share rises substantially. <cite id="d1f232cd-2">A 100% subsidiary controls dyeing/patterning/finishing and over 900 fabric suppliers</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">co-owns a key dyestuff/printing partner</cite>, so upstream conversion is largely in-house. Combined with <cite id="a764f287-1">clusters covering 95% of the chain</cite>, this indicates a majority of the value chain’s critical nodes are vertically integrated, even if not every factory is owned.
- Across stages and over time, credible summaries converge on an effective vertical integration of about 40% to 70% depending on scope and brand mix, with a conservative 40–50% figure when counting only direct ownership of garment factories and a higher 60–70% figure when including upstream fabric/dyeing control, cluster governance, and store ownership. <cite id="a764f287-1">With 12 clusters covering >95% of the chain</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">a fully owned fabric/finishing backbone</cite>, the upper end of the range is substantiated; conversely, when focusing strictly on owned final-assembly capacity and Asia-heavy sourcing, the lower end is supported. <cite id="a764f287-1">The Asia share (24%) is typically outsourced to OEMs</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-0">proximity to headquarters accounts for 59% of factories but still leaves a large external network</cite>.
- Additional triangulation: <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex’s success is explicitly attributed to vertical integration and forward integration, supported by minimal inventory and rapid data flow across design–procurement–production–distribution</cite>. This reinforces that while not fully integrated, the portion of the chain Inditex owns or tightly controls is large enough to dominate lead-time and inventory performance.

Limitations and why a single percentage is elusive
- <cite id="d1f232cd-0">Annual reports and case studies use different taxonomies (e.g., “own network” vs. “work with” vs. “cluster coverage”), and coverage definitions vary by brand (Zara vs. Massimo Dutti vs. Pull&Bear) and by category (basics vs. seasonal fashion)</cite>. 
- <cite id="a764f287-0">Some counts enumerate 11 wholly owned enterprises for preproduction but do not fully capture the share of outsourced garment volume</cite>. 
- <cite id="d1f232cd-2">Upstream integration is often measured by owned/controlled entities (Comditel, co-owned dyestuff/printing) rather than by factory ownership counts</cite>. 
- <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Company materials stress responsiveness and integration mechanisms (data, RFID, store ownership) rather than publishing a headline “X% vertically integrated” metric</cite>.

Bottom line
- If the question asks for a single percentage, a defensible range is:
  - Owned/final-assembly share: about 15–30% (often under 50%), given reliance on European owned capacity plus outsourced Asia-heavy garment output. <cite id="a764f287-0">Internal factories are concentrated in preproduction and complement a large external garment base</cite> <cite id="a764f287-1">50% Spain, 26% Europe, 24% Asia manufacturing split</cite>.
  - Effective vertical integration across critical nodes (materials, process, planning, retail): about 60–70%, since <cite id="d1f232cd-2">fabric sourcing and dyeing/patterning/finishing are largely in-house via a 100% subsidiary and co-owned partners</cite>, <cite id="a764f287-1">regional clusters cover 95% of the chain</cite>, and <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">store ownership and unified data systems tightly couple design–manufacturing–retail</cite>. A pragmatic point estimate is 50–60% for “vertically integrated” by ownership/control-weighted measures, acknowledging Inditex’s hybrid model. <cite id="a764f287-1">With clusters spanning 95% of production and 50% of items made in owned European factories</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">fully owned fabric/finishing backbone</cite>, a 50–60% range captures the empirical literature. <cite id="2f9a0f46-2">Inditex emphasizes vertical and forward integration as core to its quick-response, low-inventory model</cite>.

What would resolve the ambiguity
- A current Inditex annual report or investor deck with a clear definition (e.g., “percentage of capacity produced in wholly owned factories” or “percentage of suppliers owned/controlled at each tier”) and brand- and region-stratified numbers. Until then, combining owned factory shares, cluster coverage, and in-house materials/finishing control yields the best-supported range. <cite id="a764f287-1">Cluster coverage over 95% of the chain</cite> and <cite id="d1f232cd-2">in-house materials/finishing control</cite> together with <cite id="a764f287-1">50% Spain/26% Europe production in Inditex’s own network</cite> underpin the 50–60% ownership/control-weighted benchmark figure. </answer>

About 20% of the company's total production is premade, while 80% is produced according to the market response. Inditex can bring a new product from conceptdesign-production-store shelves in 3 weeks, which makes the company able to offer customers fresh assortments of product lines according to the market demand (Inditex Annual Report 2019).

Title: Fast Fashion Supply Chain Issues in the New Marketing Environment: Zara
Snippet: Inditex 's clothing production process can be crudely split into the following two categories: outsourced manufacturing and in-house manufacture, using Inditex's sub-brand Zara as an example. 

Inditex-supply Zara's chain network is strongly linked with its supply-side clusters thanks to the brand's extraordinary global reach. With its own sourcing staff or reliable third-party agents, the brand can operate near its design destinations thanks to this strong link, giving it the opportunity to quickly adjust garment quantities in reaction to any new trend changes or make offers. 

Zara has successfully vertically integrated this portion of its internal manufacturing, enabling the company to manage seasonal fluctuations that affect output without wholly relying on third-party manufacturing facilities. 11 totally owned enterprises make up the internal production lines. Most of these ancillary factories are utilized largely for pre-production activities like textile cutting. 100 layers of fabric will be efficiently preprocessed using robotic knives and laser cutters by computers before being transmitted to the partner's manufacturing network (Ghemawat & Nueno, 2006) [7]. 

The next element is Zara's outsourced production, which blends an effective supply chain with a flexible supply chain. 

Responsive: Zara outsources a portion of their production line to Turkey, Bulgaria, Portugal, and other surrounding regions in order to reduce the time between placing an order and receiving it. And thanks to industrial development, these localities frequently have higher industrial output capability. Inditex will incur greater production expenses and experience more flexibility if they outsource to them. Therefore, these flexible supply chains are tasked with producing high-end fashion items as well as a few tailored clothing items. 

Efficient: In labor-intensive regions like China, India, and Vietnam, Zara outsources production chores to OEMs. These facilities offer the benefit of cheaper labor costs and being nearer to the source of raw materials, but they necessitate lengthier delivery wait times for brands. As a result, they are employed to handle lengthy orders for the usual good with price-sensitive characteristics.

Title: Super Responsive Supply Chain: The Case of Spanish Fast Fashion Retailer Inditex-Zara
Snippet: Inditex works with a total of 1805 supplier situated in 53 countries. 59% of the 6959 factories Inditex works with, in total are in proximity to their headquarters in Arteixo (A Coruña, Spain), mainly in Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Morocco which also form among major production centers (Inditex Annual Report, 2016). The fashion category apparel products are sourced from these proximate factories. The rest 41 % factories are located in Asian regions (e.g. China, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Cambodia, and Vietnam) and South-American region (e.g. Brazil and Argentina) from where basic category apparel is sourced (Ferdows et al., 2004 andDriscoll &Wang., 2009). 50% of all items are manufactured in its own network of Spanish factories, 26% from Europe (e.g. Portugal, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Romania) and 24% in Asia (e.g. China, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam) and Africa (e.g. Turkey and Morocco) (Amed & Abnett, 2015). Inditex currently has 12 local dialogue platforms or geographic 'clusters' located in their sourcing regions i.e. Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Turkey, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Cambodia, China, Brazil and Argentina. These clusters encompass over 95% of Inditex's production chain (Inditex Annual Report, 2017). Each cluster is a group of stakeholders based in the same geographical region comprising of suppliers, manufacturers, trade unions, international purchasers and local Inditex CSR teams. Cluster strategy spurs collaboration between the different agents involved, significantly enhance the productivity of local manufacturers, and enable Inditex to share technology with them as a source of competitive advantage (Inditex Annual Report, 2017). Additionally, these clusters offer opportunities for cooperation with suppliers and are devised to advocate a more sustainable supply chain and production environment within a core geographic region. As such Inditex is successfully able to deploy strict social compliance and labor standards which ought to be followed by its suppliers locally and thus makes sure its suppliers' business activities have a positive impact on their communities.

snippet.text:
Inditex 's clothing production process can be crudely split into the following two categories: outsourced manufacturing and in-house manufacture, using Inditex's sub-brand Zara as an example. 

Inditex-supply Zara's chain network is strongly linked with its supply-side clusters thanks to the brand's extraordinary global reach. With its own sourcing staff or reliable third-party agents, the brand can operate near its design destinations thanks to this strong link, giving it the opportunity to quickly adjust garment quantities in reaction to any new trend changes or make offers. 

Zara has successfully vertically integrated this portion of its internal manufacturing, enabling the company to manage seasonal fluctuations that affect output without wholly relying on third-party manufacturing facilities. 11 totally owned enterprises make up the internal production lines. Most of these ancillary factories are utilized largely for pre-production activities like textile cutting. 100 layers of fabric will be efficiently preprocessed using robotic knives and laser cutters by computers before being transmitted to the partner's manufacturing network (Ghemawat & Nueno, 2006) [7]. 

The next element is Zara's outsourced production, which blends an effective supply chain with a flexible supply chain. 

Responsive: Zara outsources a portion of their production line to Turkey, Bulgaria, Portugal, and other surrounding regions in order to reduce the time between placing an order and receiving it. And thanks to industrial development, these localities frequently have higher industrial output capability. Inditex will incur greater production expenses and experience more flexibility if they outsource to them. Therefore, these flexible supply chains are tasked with producing high-end fashion items as well as a few tailored clothing items. 

Efficient: In labor-intensive regions like China, India, and Vietnam, Zara outsources production chores to OEMs. These facilities offer the benefit of cheaper labor costs and being nearer to the source of raw materials, but they necessitate lengthier delivery wait times for brands. As a result, they are employed to handle lengthy orders for the usual good with price-sensitive characteristics.

Title: Super Responsive Supply Chain: The Case of Spanish Fast Fashion Retailer Inditex-Zara
Snippet: Inditex works with a total of 1805 supplier situated in 53 countries. 59% of the 6959 factories Inditex works with, in total are in proximity to their headquarters in Arteixo (A Coruña, Spain), mainly in Spain, Portugal, Turkey and Morocco which also form among major production centers (Inditex Annual Report, 2016). The fashion category apparel products are sourced from these proximate factories. The rest 41 % factories are located in Asian regions (e.g. China, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Cambodia, and Vietnam) and South-American region (e.g. Brazil and Argentina) from where basic category apparel is sourced (Ferdows et al., 2004 andDriscoll &Wang., 2009). 50% of all items are manufactured in its own network of Spanish factories, 26% from Europe (e.g. Portugal, Bulgaria, Lithuania, Romania) and 24% in Asia (e.g. China, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Vietnam) and Africa (e.g. Turkey and Morocco) (Amed & Abnett, 2015). Each cluster is a group of stakeholders based in the same geographical region comprising of suppliers, manufacturers, trade unions, international purchasers and local Inditex CSR teams. Additionally, these clusters offer opportunities for cooperation with suppliers and are devised to advocate a more sustainable supply chain and production environment within a core geographic region. As such Inditex is successfully able to deploy strict social compliance and labor standards which ought to be followed by its suppliers locally and thus makes sure its suppliers' business activities have a positive impact on their communities.

Zara also collaborates with Fibracolor (a dyestuff producer part owned by Inditex and Zara purchases 20% of its output) to facilitate rapid changes in its printing and dyeing operations.
